exampleAnswers.title: Solving Linear Congruences by Trial and Error

question.text: Solve the linear congruence $3x \equiv 4 \:(\text{mod}\:7)$ using trial and error. Express your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $7.$
question.explanation:
Since the modulus $n=7$ is fairly small, we can solve the congruence by trial and error.

Substituting $x = 0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ into the congruence, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} 3 \cdot 0 &\equiv 0 \not\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:7) && {\color{red}\times} \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 1 &\equiv 3 \not\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:7) && {\color{red}\times} \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 2 &\equiv 6\not\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:7) && {\color{red}\times} \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 3 &\equiv 9\equiv 7+2\equiv 2 \not\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:7) && {\color{red}\times} \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 4 &\equiv 12 \equiv 7+5 \equiv 5 \not\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:7) && {\color{red}\times} \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 5 &\equiv 15 \equiv 2\cdot 7 + 1 \equiv 1 \not\equiv 4&& (\text{mod}\:7) &&{\color{red}\times}\\[5pt] 3 \cdot {\color{blue}{6}} &\equiv 18 \equiv 2\cdot 7 + 4 \equiv 4&& (\text{mod}\:7) &&{\color{green}\checkmark} \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x\equiv {\color{blue}{6}} \:(\text{mod}\:7).$

Note: Any number congruent to $6$ modulo $7$ is a solution. For example, note that $13\equiv 6,$ and this also satisfies our congruence:

\begin{align*} 3x &\equiv 3\cdot 13 \quad&&(\text{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] &\equiv 39 \quad&&(\text{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] &\equiv 5\cdot 7 + 4 \quad&&(\text{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0 + 4 \quad&&(\text{mod}\:7) \\[5pt] &\equiv 4\:\:{\color{green}\checkmark} \quad&&(\text{mod}\:7) \end{align*}

example.title: Solving Linear Congruences by Trial and Error

question.text:
Solve the modular equation $3x \equiv 5 \:(\text{mod}\:14),$ expressing your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $14.$

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=3$ and $n=14$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(3,14)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $3\,(\textrm{mod}\:14).$ To find the inverse of $3\,(\textrm{mod}\:14)$, we compute the exponents of $3\,(\textrm{mod}\:14)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:14)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 3^2 &\equiv 9 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] 3^3 &\equiv 9 \cdot 3 \equiv 27 \equiv 13 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] 3^4 &\equiv 13 \cdot 3 \equiv 39 \equiv 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] 3^5 &\equiv 11 \cdot 3 \equiv 33 \equiv 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] 3^6 &\equiv 5 \cdot 3 \equiv 15 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $5 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:14),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $3$ (modulo $14$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 3x &\equiv 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] 5 \cdot 3x &\equiv 5 \cdot 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] (5 \cdot 3)x &\equiv 25 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 1 \cdot 14 + 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:14) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{11} \: (\text{mod}\:14).$

question.explanation:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=7$ and $n=30$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(7,30)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $7\,(\textrm{mod}\:30).$ To find the inverse of $7\,(\textrm{mod}\:30)$, we compute the exponents of $7\,(\textrm{mod}\:30)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:30)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 7^2 &\equiv 49 \equiv 30 + 19\equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{19} && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] 7^3 &\equiv 19 \cdot 7 \equiv 133 \equiv 4\cdot 30+ 13 \equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{13} && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] 7^4 &\equiv 13 \cdot 7 \equiv 91 \equiv 3\cdot 30 + 1\equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1} && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $13 \cdot 7 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:30),$ which means that $13$ is the multiplicative inverse of $7$ (modulo $30$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $13,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 7x &\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] 13 \cdot 7x &\equiv 13 \cdot 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] (13 \cdot 7)x &\equiv 78 && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 2 \cdot 30 + 18 && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 18 && (\textrm{mod}\:30) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{18} \: (\text{mod}\:30).$

question.text:
Solve the following congruence: \[ 5x - 4 \equiv 34 \quad (\text{mod}\:18) \]

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
First, we reduce our congruence to a congruence of the form $ax\equiv b,$ as follows: \begin{align*} 5x - 4 &\equiv 34 \quad &(\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5x - 4 + 4 &\equiv 34 + 4 \quad &(\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 38 \quad &(\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 2\cdot 18 + 2 \quad &(\text{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 2 \quad &(\text{mod}\:18) \end{align*}

Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=5$ and $n=18$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(5,18)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:18).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:18)$, we compute the exponents of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:18)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:18)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 5^2 &\equiv 25 \equiv 1 \cdot 18 + 7 \equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^3 &\equiv 7 \cdot 5 \equiv 35 \equiv 1 \cdot 18 + 17 \equiv 17&& (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^4 &\equiv 17 \cdot 5 \equiv 85 \equiv 4 \cdot 18 + 13 \equiv 13 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^5 &\equiv 13 \cdot 5 \equiv 65 \equiv 3\cdot 18 + 11 \equiv 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^6 &\equiv 11 \cdot 5 \equiv 55 \equiv 3 \cdot 18 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $11 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:18),$ which means that $11$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $18$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $11,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 11 \cdot 5x &\equiv 11 \cdot 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] (11 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 22 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 4 + 1 \cdot 18 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv 4\: (\text{mod}\:18).$

question.text:
Solve the following congruence \[ 5x + 3 \equiv 22 \quad (\text{mod}\:12), \] expressing your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $12.$

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
First, we reduce our congruence to a congruence of the form $ax\equiv b,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 5x + 3 &\equiv 22 \quad &(\text{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] 5x + 3 - 3 &\equiv 22-3 \quad &(\text{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 19 \quad &(\text{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 1 \cdot 12 + 7 \quad &(\text{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] 5x &\equiv 7 \quad &(\text{mod}\:12) \end{align*}

Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=5$ and $n=12$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(5,12)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:12).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:12)$, we compute the exponents of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:12)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:12)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 5^2 &\equiv 25 \equiv 2 \cdot 12 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $5 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:12),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $12$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] 5 \cdot 5x &\equiv 5 \cdot 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] (5 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 35 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 11 + 2 \cdot 12 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:12) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{11} \: (\text{mod}\:12).$

question.text:
Solve the following congruence: \[ 9x - 22 \equiv 7 \quad (\text{mod}\:11) \]

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
First, we reduce our congruence to a congruence of the form $ax\equiv b,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 9x - 22 &\equiv 7 \quad &(\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9x - 22 + 22 &\equiv 7 + 22 \quad &(\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9x &\equiv 29 \quad &(\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9x &\equiv 2\cdot 11 + 7 \quad &(\text{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9x &\equiv 7 \quad &(\text{mod}\:11) \end{align*}

Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=9$ and $n=11$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(9,11)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $9\,(\textrm{mod}\:11).$ To find the inverse of $9\,(\textrm{mod}\:11)$, we compute the exponents of $9\,(\textrm{mod}\:11)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:11)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 9^2 &\equiv 81 \equiv 7 \cdot 11 + 4 \equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9^3 &\equiv 4 \cdot 9 \equiv 36 \equiv 3 \cdot 11 + 3 \equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9^4 &\equiv 3 \cdot 9 \equiv 27 \equiv 2 \cdot 11 + 5 \equiv 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 9^5 &\equiv 5\cdot 9 \equiv 45 \equiv 4\cdot 11 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $5 \cdot 9 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:11),$ which means that $5$ is the multiplicative inverse of $9$ (modulo $11$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 9x &\equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 5 \cdot 9x &\equiv 5 \cdot 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] (5 \cdot 9)x &\equiv 35 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 2 + 3 \cdot 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv 2\: (\text{mod}\:11).$

In the given congruence, we have $a=5$ and $n=18$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(5,18)=1. \]

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:18).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:18)$, we compute the exponents of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:18)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:18)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 5^2 &\equiv 25 \equiv 1 \cdot 18 + 7 \equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^3 &\equiv 7 \cdot 5 \equiv 35 \equiv 1 \cdot 18 + 17 \equiv 17 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^4 &\equiv 17 \cdot 5 \equiv 85 \equiv 4 \cdot 18 + 13 \equiv 13 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^5 &\equiv 13 \cdot 5 \equiv 65 \equiv 3\cdot 18 + 11 \equiv 11 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 5^6 &\equiv 11 \cdot 5 \equiv 55 \equiv 3 \cdot 18 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $11 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:18),$ which means that $11$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $18$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $11,$ we get the following: \begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 11 \cdot 5x &\equiv 11 \cdot 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] (11 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 77 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 5 + 4 \cdot 18 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:18) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv 5\: (\text{mod}\:18).$

question.text:
Solve the following congruence \[ 4x - 25 \equiv 20 \quad (\text{mod}\:21), \] expressing your answer as a nonnegative integer smaller than $21.$

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
First, we reduce our congruence to a congruence of the form $ax\equiv b,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 4x - 25 &\equiv 20 \quad &(\text{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 4x - 25 + 25 &\equiv 20 + 25 \quad &(\text{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 4x &\equiv 45 \quad &(\text{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 4x &\equiv 2 \cdot 21 + 3 \quad &(\text{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 4x &\equiv 3 \quad &(\text{mod}\:21) \end{align*}

Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=4$ and $n=21$, and \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(4,21)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $4\,(\textrm{mod}\:21).$ To find the inverse of $4\,(\textrm{mod}\:21)$, we compute the exponents of $4\,(\textrm{mod}\:21)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:21)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 4^2 & \equiv 16 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 4^3 & \equiv 16 \cdot 4 \equiv 64 \equiv 3\cdot 21 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \end{align*}

So, $16 \cdot 4 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:21),$ which means that $16$ is the multiplicative inverse of $4$ (modulo $21$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $16,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 4x &\equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 16 \cdot 4x &\equiv 16 \cdot 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] (16 \cdot 4)x &\equiv 48 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 6 + 2 \cdot 21 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:21) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{6}\: (\text{mod}\:21).$

question.text: Solve the congruence $22x \equiv 5 \:(\text{mod}\:31).$
question.explanation:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=22$ and $n=31$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(22,31)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $22\,(\textrm{mod}\:31).$ To find the inverse of $22\,(\textrm{mod}\:31)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}31 & = & \color{red}22 \cdot1 & + & \color{red}9 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}22 & = & \color{blue}9 \cdot 2 & + & \color{blue}4 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ 9 & = & 4 \cdot 2 & + & 1 \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}9 &= \color{red}31 - 22 \\[5pt] \color{blue}4 &= \color{blue}22 - 9\cdot 2 \\[5pt] 1 &= 9 - 4\cdot 2. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 9-{\color{blue}4}\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 9 - {\color{blue}(22-9\cdot 2)}\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}9} \cdot 5 - 22\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}(31-22)} \cdot 5 - 22\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 31 \cdot 5 - 22 \cdot 7 \\[5pt] &=31 \cdot 5 + 22 \cdot (-7) \end{align*}

So, we have \[ 1 = 31 \cdot 5 + 22 \cdot (-7). \] We can write this result in modulo $31,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 31 \cdot 5 + 22 \cdot (-7)&\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] 22 \cdot (-7) &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] 22 \cdot (31-7) &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] 22 \cdot 24 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $22 \cdot 24 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:31),$ which means that $24$ is the multiplicative inverse of $22$ (modulo $31$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $24,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 22x &\equiv 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] 24 \cdot 22x &\equiv 24 \cdot 5 && (\textrm{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] (24 \cdot 22)x &\equiv 120 && (\textrm{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 3\cdot 31 + 27 && (\textrm{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 27 && (\textrm{mod}\:31) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv 27 \: (\text{mod}\:31).$

question.text: Solve the congruence $14x \equiv 6 \:(\text{mod}\:55).$
question.explanation:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=14$ and $n=55$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(14,55)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $14\,(\textrm{mod}\:55).$ To find the inverse of $14\,(\textrm{mod}\:55)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}55 & = & \color{red}14 \cdot 3 & + & \color{red}13 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}14 & = & \color{blue}13 \cdot 1 & + & \color{blue}1 \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}13 &= \color{red}55 - 14 \cdot 3 \\[5pt] \color{blue}1 &= \color{blue}14 - 13 \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} \color{blue}1 &= {\color{blue}14}-{\color{red}13} \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}14} - {\color{red}(55-14 \cdot 3 )} \\[5pt] &= 14 \cdot 4 - 55 \end{align*}

We can write this result in modulo $55,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 14\cdot 4 -55 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:55)\\[5pt] 14 \cdot 4 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:55)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $14 \cdot 4 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:55),$ which means that $4$ is the multiplicative inverse of $14$ (modulo $55$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $4,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 14x &\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:55) \\[5pt] 4 \cdot 14x &\equiv 4 \cdot 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:55) \\[5pt] (4 \cdot 14)x &\equiv 24 && (\textrm{mod}\:55) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 24 && (\textrm{mod}\:55) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 24 && (\textrm{mod}\:55) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv 24 \: (\text{mod}\:55).$

question.text: Solve the congruence $17x \equiv 9 \:(\text{mod}\:50).$
question.explanation:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In the given congruence, we have $a=17$ and $n=50$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(17,50)=1. \] So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $17\,(\textrm{mod}\:50).$ To find the inverse of $17\,(\textrm{mod}\:50)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}50 & = & \color{red}17 \cdot 2 & + & \color{red}16 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}17 & = & \color{blue}16 \cdot 1 & + & \color{blue}1 \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}16 &= \color{red}50 - 17 \cdot 2 \\[5pt] \color{blue}1 &= \color{blue}17 - 16 \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} \color{blue}1 &= {\color{blue}17}-{\color{red}16} \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}17} - {\color{red}(50-17 \cdot 2 )} \\[5pt] &= 17 \cdot 3 - 50 \end{align*}

We can write this result in modulo $50,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 17\cdot 3 -50 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:50)\\[5pt] 17 \cdot 3 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:50)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, $17 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:50),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $17$ (modulo $50$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 17x &\equiv 9 && (\textrm{mod}\:50) \\[5pt] 3 \cdot 17x &\equiv 3 \cdot 9 && (\textrm{mod}\:50) \\[5pt] (3 \cdot 17)x &\equiv 27 && (\textrm{mod}\:50) \\[5pt] 1\cdot x &\equiv 27 && (\textrm{mod}\:50) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 27 && (\textrm{mod}\:50) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is $x \equiv 27 \: (\text{mod}\:50).$
